label: Chapter 2: Dukes, Guilds and the Grand Place, 1100 to 1430

units.text: In the twelfth century, Brussels came into the hands of an ambitious family that would turn a market town into the capital of a duchy.
The counts of Leuven, who held Brussels, steadily rose in rank.
They became dukes of Lower Lotharingia, and then, as the old title lost its meaning, dukes of Brabant.
The duchy of Brabant was one of the richest territories in northwest Europe.
It stretched across the heart of what is now Belgium and part of the southern Netherlands, and it included great towns like Leuven, Antwerp, and Brussels.
For a long time, Leuven was the leading city.
But gradually the dukes spent more time in Brussels, in a castle on the hill called the Coudenberg, which means cold hill.
By the late Middle Ages, Brussels was the main seat of the dukes, and with the dukes came money, officials, and prestige.
But Brussels owed its growth just as much to its own people.
The town made cloth. Wool came in from England, weavers and dyers worked it into fabric, and merchants sold it across Europe.
Alongside the cloth trade grew many other crafts: brewing, baking, butchery, metalwork, carpentry, and eventually luxury goods like tapestries.
The people who practiced these trades organized themselves into guilds, which were part trade union, part business association, part social club, and part political party.
At the center of it all was the market.
Down in the valley, on low ground close to the river, there was an open space known as the Lower Market.
It was a place for traders to set up stalls and for townspeople to meet and do business.
Over the centuries, wooden stalls turned into stone halls, and the guilds built meeting houses around the edges.
That muddy field is the Grand Place, the great square at the heart of Brussels today.
By the end of the thirteenth century, the drapers' guild had its own hall there, and the foundation of the square's future was laid.
Politically, the town was run by a narrow elite.
Power lay in the hands of a few wealthy families, known as the Seven Lineages of Brussels, who held the city council and the best offices.
Below them were the guilds, which had economic muscle but little say in government.
This was a recipe for tension, and over time it boiled over.
Here is where we meet one of the great documents of Brussels history.
In 1355, the Duke of Brabant, John the Third, died without a male heir.

His eldest daughter, Joanna, became duchess, and her husband was a man we have met before if you listened to our story of Luxembourg: Wenceslas of Luxembourg, the half brother of the Emperor Charles the Fourth.
In January of 1356, before they could take up their rule, Joanna and Wenceslas had to sign a charter promising to respect the rights of the towns and nobles of Brabant.
This charter is called the Joyous Entry.
It was named for the ceremonial entry that a new ruler made into the cities of the duchy.
The Joyous Entry laid out limits on the power of the duke.

He could not declare war, sign treaties, or raise taxes without the consent of the estates, and the charter included a remarkable clause that allowed the people of Brabant to withdraw their obedience if the duke broke the rules.
It is often compared to the Magna Carta in England.

Historians caution that its later reputation was somewhat exaggerated by romantic writers of the nineteenth century, but it remained an important symbol for centuries, and Brabantine rulers swore to uphold it for generations.
Almost immediately, the charter was tested.
Louis of Male, the Count of Flanders, a powerful neighbor with his own claim to Brabant, invaded and seized Brussels in 1356.
But he did not hold it for long.
A citizen of Brussels named Everard t'Serclaes, from one of the great families, led a night raid with a small band of men, slipped into the city, and drove out the Flemish garrison.
Everard became a folk hero. He was killed by a rival lord a few decades later, and today a bronze monument to him lies against a wall just off the Grand Place.
According to local custom, rubbing the bronze arm of the statue brings good luck, and you will see that the metal is polished bright by the hands of passersby.
The liberation of Brussels helped fuel another great project.
With the city growing quickly, the old walls had become too small.
Between 1356 and 1383, the people of Brussels built a second, much larger ring of walls, with seven main gates and dozens of towers.
This wall was a huge undertaking for a town of this size.
It enclosed about eight kilometers of ground and made room for the city to expand.
Most of it was torn down in the nineteenth century, and its path is now traced by a ring of boulevards around the old center, known as the Petite Ceinture, or the small ring.
If you look at a map of central Brussels, the five-sided shape of the boulevards is the outline of the old medieval city.
One gate survives, the heavy, castle-like Porte de Hal, on the southern side of the ring.
The early fifteenth century was the great age of civic building.
In 1402, work began on the Brussels Town Hall, on the Grand Place.
The left wing was built first, and the right wing followed in the 1440s.
In 1449 the architects began the soaring tower, a lace of stone that rises about ninety-six meters, topped by a gilded statue of Saint Michael slaying the dragon.
A famous detail is that the tower is not centered above the main doorway of the building, and the wings are of slightly different lengths.
According to an old story, the architect was so horrified by the asymmetry that he threw himself from the tower.
Historians think that is just a legend, but it is a good one.
There is another city landmark from this period, and it is the smallest.
A fountain figure of a little boy, relieving himself into a basin, is first mentioned in a document from 1388.

It is the Manneken Pis. The bronze statue you can visit today is a copy of a version made in 1619 by the sculptor Jérôme Duquesnoy, and it stands on a street corner a few minutes from the Grand Place.
The boy has become an icon, and he has a wardrobe of well over a thousand costumes, which are changed regularly on special occasions.
Many legends try to explain him.
In one, a small duke of Leuven, hung in a basket from a tree during a battle, urinated on the enemy and inspired his soldiers.
In another, a boy put out a burning fuse and saved the city.
No one knows the real story, and Brussels does not mind.
Meanwhile, the tension between the Seven Lineages and the guilds finally exploded in 1421.
A group of guildsmen, angry about the patricians' control of the government and rising taxes, stormed the town hall, and several city magistrates were killed.
The duke, John the Fourth, intervened to restore order, but the result was a victory for the craftsmen.
From then on, the guilds, organized into nine groups known as the Nations of Brussels, had a formal share of power on the city council.
For the first time, Brussels had a government in which ordinary working people had a say.
In the same period, the dynasty that ruled the duchy kept changing.
Wenceslas died in 1383 without children.

Joanna lived until 1406 and left the duchy to her grandnephew, a son of the powerful Duke of Burgundy, and from then on, Brabant's rulers were a succession of Burgundian princes, one of whom was killed at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415.
The family line died out. And in 1430, the duchy fell to the most powerful of all of them: Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.
If you are out walking in Brussels, here is what to look for.
On the Grand Place, look up at the Town Hall tower and notice that it is off-center.
Then walk a few steps to the Rue Charles Buls, just off the square, to find the monument to Everard t'Serclaes.
And a few streets farther, you will find the Manneken Pis, surprisingly small, usually surrounded by a crowd.
In the next chapter, Brussels becomes the capital of an empire.
